description: We are a team of curious minds, united by a passion for space exploration and technology. We all are currently pursuing our master's degrees in aerospace engineering at the University of Toronto.
summary: We developed an interactive HTML-based visualization of the Martian surface to help users explore and assess potential landing sites on Mars. The tool allows future researchers, scientists, and space exploration enthusiasts to examine the distribution of impact craters across the Martian terrain and identify regions with fewer nearby craters. By highlighting areas that may offer safer landing conditions, the project aims to support preliminary landing-site assessment and contribute to the planning of future Mars exploration missions. This is important because selecting a suitable landing site is a critical aspect of mission planning, where understanding the surrounding terrain and potential hazards can help reduce risks to spacecraft and future exploration activities.
details:
As humanity extends its horizons beyond Earth and towards Mars, identifying suitable landing sites for future spacecraft and astronauts becomes increasingly important. Our motivation to explore this challenge stemmed from lunar exploration. Since the Moon lacks an atmosphere, its surface is exposed to frequent meteorite impacts, making the distribution and severity of impact craters an important consideration when assessing potential landing sites. We wanted to extend this line of thinking to Mars, whose surface also features numerous impact craters, mountains, and other geographical features that could pose challenges during landing.

To address this, we developed an interactive map of the Martian surface that allows users to explore specific regions, draw a rectangular selection around an area of interest, and assess the surrounding impact crater distribution to help identify potentially safer landing zones. We primarily used Python for the development of the tool, along with HTML to create the interactive interface. The project's creative aspect lies in making geographical data more accessible and interactive, allowing users to independently investigate different regions of Mars rather than relying solely on static maps or visual references. Ultimately, we hope this tool can serve as a useful starting point for preliminary landing-site assessments and contribute to the broader goal of making future Mars exploration safer.
